explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF sends row-count messages for statements in the procedure, adding avoidable client traffic.
With XACT_ABORT OFF, some run-time errors can leave an explicit transaction open instead of rolling it back.
@CustomerIdText is initialized to a fixed customer ID rather than using an input.
@OrderID starts at the fixed order ID 1, which is used by the arithmetic predicate before any lookup.
SELECT * returns every Sales.Orders column, including large text fields, and makes the result shape depend on the table schema.
TOP (10) does not specify which orders to return.
Sales.Orders.OrderID is the primary key, so DISTINCT cannot remove any duplicates.
NOLOCK on Sales.Orders can read uncommitted data and can miss or duplicate rows during concurrent writes.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) makes the filter non-sargable; it does not express a direct range on OrderDate.
The OrderDate filter embeds the reporting year 2016 instead of accepting a year or date range as input.
The int CustomerID comparison implicitly converts the nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText to int. The current value converts, but nonnumeric values would fail.
The OR predicate combines a CustomerID lookup with an unfiltered case, which can make it harder to choose an efficient plan for both.
The leading wildcard in N'%urgent%' requires a substring search of Orders.Comments rather than a prefix seek.
ISNULL wraps the indexed CustomerID and is redundant because Sales.Orders.CustomerID is NOT NULL.
The filter selects the fixed customer ID 1 instead of using @CustomerID.
Adding zero to OrderID does not alter the comparison and obscures a direct equality predicate on the primary key.
CustomerID <> 1 excludes only one customer and can read most of Sales.Orders.
The exclusion embeds customer ID 1 without naming or parameterizing that business choice.
The CROSS JOIN can pair an order with a customer unrelated to that order.
TOP (1) does not specify which order and customer pair to return.
The comma-separated FROM clause puts the Orders-to-OrderLines join condition in WHERE instead of an explicit JOIN.
TOP (1) returns an arbitrary OrderID from the joined rows.
LineCount is calculated through a scalar count correlated to each order. Preaggregating OrderLines by OrderID can avoid repeated lookups.
The quantity test is expressed as a correlated EXISTS. It can also be joined to a set of distinct qualifying OrderIDs, although SQL Server may already use a semi-join.
The minimum line quantity is embedded as 1 with no named threshold.
The Comments CASE expression is repeated in ORDER BY even though the HasComments alias is available.
ORDER BY 2 sorts by OrderDate only as long as OrderDate remains the second select-list expression.
OrderDate is not unique. Without a tie-breaker such as OrderID, orders with the same date can shift between pages.
Each branch selects a different primary-key value, so UNION duplicate elimination is unnecessary.
The first UNION branch embeds order ID 1.
The second UNION branch embeds order ID 2.
COUNT(*) > 0 counts matching order lines even though the predicate only needs to know whether one exists.
The assignment reads all orders and leaves @OrderID with whichever value is processed last. If there are no orders, it retains its previous value.
The insert into @OrderIds does not define which five order IDs to keep.
SELECT INTO infers the schema of #ImplicitOrders from the query rather than declaring it explicitly.
The query does not define which five orders populate #ImplicitOrders.
The cursor is opened for a single FETCH into @OrderID. A direct scalar query can retrieve that row without cursor setup and cleanup.
The statement converts @CustomerID to text and embeds it in the SQL, producing different statement text for different customer IDs.
EXEC runs the generated customer lookup without binding @CustomerID as a typed parameter.
The statement embeds @OrderID in executable text instead of keeping the query text fixed.
sys.sp_executesql receives only the SQL text, leaving the order ID embedded instead of binding it as a parameter.
#Scratch is explicitly created but not explicitly dropped; SQL Server cleans it up when the procedure scope ends.
The CATCH block returns an error message as a result row but does not rethrow or signal failure to the caller.
The negative-order-ID path uses RAISERROR, which does not honor SET XACT_ABORT the way THROW does.
PRINT sends a buffered, unstructured diagnostic message to the client.
The order query embeds customer ID 1 rather than using @CustomerID.
The order filter embeds January 1, 2016 as an unnamed lower bound.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') can yield January 2 or February 1 depending on the session date format.
COALESCE obscures a direct CustomerID equality join and is redundant because both CustomerID columns are NOT NULL.
TOP (1) does not specify which order to return from the invoice join.
The join matches each order to itself by primary key and retrieves no data from the second alias.
TOP (1) returns an arbitrary order even if the redundant self-join is removed.
Sorting all orders by the nvarchar(max) Comments column can be expensive in memory and tempdb.
SUM(Quantity) processes the full Sales.OrderLines table because there is no restrictive filter.
OrderID > 0 is a row-level filter on the grouping key and can be expressed in WHERE before grouping.
COUNT(*) performs an exact count over all Sales.Orders rows without a restrictive filter.
The ungrouped COUNT(*) returns one row, so ordering by OrderCount has no effect.
MERGE is unnecessary for a matched-only operation on Sales.Orders and adds complexity compared with a key-based UPDATE.
The matched clause assigns Comments to itself but can still acquire write locks and fire update triggers.
SET Comments = Comments does not change the stored value but still issues an update against Sales.Orders.
Deleting by Quantity alone can remove matching lines from many unrelated orders.
The delete treats -1 as a special quantity without naming what makes those rows eligible for deletion.
WAITFOR DELAY suspends the request for one second and occupies a worker while it waits.
The transaction starts outside TRY/CATCH, so no local error handler guarantees cleanup.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT ON fails because the supplied Sales.Orders definition has no identity column.
The call to sp_who omits its sys schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is not reset within the procedure and can silently limit subsequent queries and data changes to one row.
The VALUES insert into #DemoCategories relies on the table's physical column order.
The insert embeds category ID 99 rather than accepting or deriving the ID.
The pattern starts with %, preventing a prefix seek on the indexed Sales.Customers.CustomerName column.
@CustomerName is concatenated directly into SQL executed on the next line, so caller input can change the statement. Bind the LIKE pattern as a parameter.
The call to sp_executesql omits its sys schema qualifier.
The update has no row filter. The active ROWCOUNT limit can mask the missing predicate by restricting the update to an unspecified row.
The update assigns the fixed customer category ID 1 rather than using a named or supplied value.
The WHERE predicate on o.OrderDate rejects NULL-extended rows, so customers without a qualifying order are excluded despite the LEFT JOIN.
The join result is filtered using January 1, 2016 as an unnamed cutoff.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL does not test for missing values. Use IS NULL for that test; the supplied column definition is NOT NULL.
dbo.GetCustomerType can be evaluated separately for each customer row unless SQL Server can inline the function.
The transaction handler returns only ERROR_MESSAGE() and lets execution continue without signaling failure.
The handler does not roll back an active transaction, so a failure before COMMIT can leave the transaction open.
INDEX = 1 forces a specific access path for Sales.Customers and prevents the optimizer from choosing a better index for the name filter.
Three nested derived tables pass through CustomerID unchanged; a single query can apply the same name filter.
LIKE '%A%' searches for a substring and cannot use a prefix seek on CustomerName.
SELECT * exposes all columns returned by dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti and makes the result shape depend on the function's output schema.
